analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal housing authority to buy distressed properties and build permanently affordable social housing with tenant protections.
analysis.headline: The Homes Act of 2024 was introduced in September 2024 with three Democratic senators and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an independent Housing Development Authority inside HUD with power to buy or take over distressed and vacant properties, fix them up, and keep them as permanently affordable "social housing" — rents capped at 25% of a household's income, increases limited to 3% a year, just-cause eviction rules, and units set aside for the lowest-income families. It would give tenants and community groups the first chance to buy apartment buildings before investors, let the federal government build public housing again by repealing a 1998 ban, and require prevailing wages and project labor agreements on the resulting construction. The bill never moved past its first referral to the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-burdened tenants and families priced out of the market: at least 40% of new units would be set aside for extremely low-income families and rents would be capped at 25% of income with increases limited to 3% a year or inflation. Tenants would gain just-cause eviction protections, the right to return after renovation, and protection against discrimination based on source of income. Tenant organizations and community land trusts would get the first opportunity to purchase apartment buildings coming up for sale. Construction workers would benefit from prevailing-wage requirements and project labor agreements on large projects.

how_it_helps.text: Rents in new social housing would be capped at 25% of a household's income, with annual increases limited to the lesser of 3% or inflation, and at least 40% of units reserved for extremely low-income families.

The Authority could acquire distressed, vacant, and blighted properties by purchase, receivership, or eminent domain, rehabilitate them, and hold them permanently off the speculative market with a use restriction barring resale into the private market.

Owners of covered multifamily buildings would have to give tenants and the Authority 90 days' notice before selling, followed by a 30-day first-look period giving tenant organizations and community nonprofits priority to buy.

The bill repeals the Faircloth Amendment, a 1998 law that has blocked the federal government from building new public housing units, and authorizes funding to clear the public housing maintenance backlog.

Construction funded under the bill must pay prevailing wages, use project labor agreements on projects of $25 million or more, prefer American-made materials, and would not rely on temporary staffing agencies except in certified short-term shortages.
Residents of social housing would gain a democratic role through tenant organizations with automatic bargaining rights and six resident seats on the Authority's 15-member board.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the Authority's operations and the public housing backlog through annual appropriations, and the federal government would guarantee the Authority's bonds. Owners of distressed and covered multifamily properties would bear costs through the 90-day notice and first-look requirements, eminent domain acquisitions, purchase-price limits tied to outstanding debt, and a 2% annual cap on profit for any limited-equity stakes in conveyed properties.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes appropriations for both the Authority and a public housing backlog but leaves the amounts to future Congresses, so the full fiscal cost would be set later.

The Authority's power of eminent domain — including when tenants petition it or when a state or local government is blocking affordable housing — would let the federal government take private property, a use critics of eminent domain broadly consider ripe for overreach even with the bill's anti-displacement limits.

Deep rent caps (25% of income) with limits on increases can produce long waiting lists and require ongoing operating subsidies, and the bill would make the Authority independent from the HUD Secretary's review, raising accountability questions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tenant protections and set-asides directly target the households with the worst housing cost burdens, and permanent affordability is a structural fix rather than a subsidy that expires. But the model is expensive: it relies on federal appropriations and federally guaranteed bonds, its rent formula requires operating subsidies to stay solvent, and its eminent domain and independence provisions are significant expansions of federal power that reasonable people would want narrower. The scale of the housing problem it addresses is large, but so is the fiscal and governance commitment it demands.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and died there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the Homes Act of 2024 on September 18, 2024, joined by Senators Peter Welch and Jeff Merkley.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the action history ends with the committee referral, with no hearing, markup, floor vote, or companion House action.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill; it would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of multifamily rental housing and distressed-property investors are better off because the bill died: no federal authority now competes for their acquisitions, and their buildings carry no first-look sale obligations or profit caps. Rent-burdened tenants gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Homes Act of 2024 and led its sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs (Chair Sherrod Brown)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached the floor for a test vote.

industries.industry: Multifamily landlords and real estate investors
industries.note: The bill would let the Authority buy or seize distressed and vacant rental properties, force 90-day notice and a tenant-first chance to buy before buildings are sold, and cap profit on conveyed property at 2% a year. Its core goal — permanently affordable housing outside the speculative market — exists precisely to shrink the market investors rely on.

industries.industry: Nonprofit housing developers, community land trusts, and tenant organizations
industries.note: They are the designated eligible entities that would receive properties and financing from the Authority to run permanently affordable housing, with limits on their own future profits.

The bill directs public spending to construction with prevailing wages, mandatory project labor agreements on projects of $25 million or more, Buy America materials, and limits on temporary staffing hires — provisions that favor organized, higher-road contractors and their workforce.

industries.industry: Institutional investors and banks holding federal-guaranteed bonds
industries.note: The Authority's bonds would be guaranteed by the United States and made legal investments for savings banks, trust funds, and insurance companies, creating a new safe asset for institutional buyers.
